title: Preparation geometry and slow-sector routing in driven Kerr resonators: an operational spectral theory of Liouvillians
abstract: Liouvillian eigenvalues determine decay rates and oscillation frequencies, but not how the corresponding modes are excited, propagated, and detected in a chosen protocol. We develop an operational spectral theory based on matched left and right eigenoperators. Left eigenoperators determine excitation by an input or source; right eigenoperators determine the propagated density deformation and readout overlap; their product is a gauge-invariant modal weight. For bosonic systems, coherent preparations turn left eigenoperators into phase-space excitation maps whose zeros identify mode-selective suppression, while right eigenoperators yield the corresponding Wigner deformations. Resolved slow subspaces define operational coordinates and, when positivity and Markov-admissibility hold, a projected routing generator. In driven Kerr resonators, the framework identifies preparations that suppress a switching mode, separates symmetry-resolved relaxation channels, and reveals bias-induced crossovers in projected multichannel routing while the coherent-preparation partition continues to deform. Preparation geometry and slow-sector propagation thus provide complementary operational information beyond Liouvillian eigenvalues alone.
summary: The paper introduces an operational spectral theory for Liouvillians that moves beyond just calculating decay rates by incorporating how input sources and measurement readouts couple to the system's modes. Using this framework on driven Kerr resonators, the authors demonstrate that specific preparation geometries can suppress unwanted dynamics or isolate distinct relaxation pathways. This provides a powerful diagnostic tool for understanding complex open quantum optical systems.
main_problem: To develop an operational spectral theory for Liouvillians that characterizes not only decay rates (eigenvalues) but also precisely how quantum modes are excited, propagated, and detected in a specific experimental protocol.
main_result: The framework shows that preparation geometry and slow-sector propagation provide complementary operational information beyond just the eigenvalues, allowing identification of mode suppression and separation of relaxation channels in driven Kerr resonators.
method: The theory utilizes matched left and right eigenoperators ($\hat{\ell}_k$ and $\hat{r}_k$) associated with the Liouvillian spectrum to define an operational modal weight that governs excitation and readout overlap.
model_or_system: The study focuses on open quantum systems, specifically driven Kerr resonators, whose dynamics are governed by a Lindblad master equation derived from a Hamiltonian involving nonlinearity and external drives.
key_observables: Left/right eigenoperators ($\hat{\ell}_k, \hat{r}_k$), modal weight ($w_k$), excitation factor ($E_k$), detection factor ($D_k$), and residues ($R_{AB}^k$) for stationary correlations.
important_parameters: The Kerr nonlinearity strength ($U$), drive strengths ($F, G$), and the spectral gap/slow subspace definition are key parameters governing the dynamics.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a finite-dimensional Liouville space and often requires checking multiple conditions (positivity, trace-one) to ensure that projected reduced models remain valid Markov generators.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the operational anatomy, showing spectral features like gap modes, steady-state Wigner functions, right-mode symbols, and coherent-state excitation maps derived from the theory.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the general Liouvillian spectrum to introducing left/right eigenoperators. It then applies this framework to analyze specific physical phenomena in Kerr resonators, including mode suppression and stationary correlation analysis via residues, concluding with extensions to perturbation theory on slow manifolds.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a rigorous mathematical toolset for analyzing open quantum systems dynamics beyond simple spectral decomposition, directly linking theoretical structure (eigenoperators) to measurable experimental protocols (preparation/readout).
